content: The declared conflicts of interest were assessed and determined not to be significant enough to compromise the integrity of the guideline development process or diminish its credibility. Helen Foster, affiliated with Newcastle University in Newcastle-upon-Tyne, United Kingdom, received research funding exceeding $5,000 USD for studies on pediatric musculoskeletal conditions, including funding from private sector entities such as Pfizer, Sanofi Genzyme, and AbbVie. Due to a conflict of interest related to pharmacotherapies, she recused herself from providing comments on systemic pharmacotherapies. This conflict was not deemed significant enough to affect the guideline development process or its credibility. Helen Foster’s expertise lies in clinical practice and research in osteopathy, particularly in areas such as back pain, clinicians’ beliefs and attitudes, reassurance, communication, consent, psychologically informed practice, safety, and manual therapy. She holds a senior management position at the University College of Osteopathy and has no employment ties to the private sector. She is also self-employed, delivering continuing professional development courses to healthcare professionals, focusing on person-centered care, communication skills, adverse events, and psychologically informed interventions, including for back pain, with earnings exceeding $5,000 USD. Helen Foster has held executive committee positions for the charity Society for Back Pain Research, where she currently serves as President and Chair of Trustees. The society promotes the study of spinal pain. She was a member of the United Kingdom Spine Societies Board from 2016 to 2018 and participated in two NICE guideline development groups (2007–2009 and 2014–2016) focused on back pain. Additionally, she contributed to the development of the National Low Back and Radicular Pain Pathway in the UK from 2014 to 2017. Her declared conflicts of interest were not considered significant enough to compromise the guideline development process or its credibility. Janet Gunderson, affiliated with The Arthritis Society in Toronto, received research funding exceeding $5,000 USD, including from private sector sources, all of which was paid to the World Spine Care charity. She also received travel reimbursement for attending meetings as a committee member or speaker, though none occurred in the past 12 months. Her declared conflicts of interest were not deemed significant enough to pose a risk to the guideline development process or its credibility. Janet Gunderson also received student scholarship support from GlaxoSmithKline, amounting to less than $5,000 USD, which was paid to the University of Sydney. This conflict of interest was similarly assessed as not significant enough to affect the guideline development process or its credibility.
